title: Transpose a row-major matrix

tests.expr: ({ int s[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, d[6]; transpose(s, d, 2, 3); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[] = {1, 2, 3, 4}, d[4]; transpose(s, d, 2, 2); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[] = {7}, d[1]; transpose(s, d, 1, 1); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 1; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[] = {1, 2, 3, 4}, d[4]; transpose(s, d, 1, 4); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[] = {1, 2, 3, 4}, d[4]; transpose(s, d, 4, 1); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, d[6]; transpose(s, d, 3, 2); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[12], d[12]; for (int k = 0; k < 12; k++) s[k] = k; transpose(s, d, 3, 4); static char b[512]; int o = 0; for (int k = 0; k < 12; k++) o += snprintf(b + o, sizeof b - o, "%d ", d[k]); b; })
({ int s[12], d[12], t[12], ok = 1; for (int k = 0; k < 12; k++) s[k] = k * k - 7; transpose(s, d, 4, 3); transpose(d, t, 3, 4); for (int k = 0; k < 12; k++) ok &= t[k] == s[k]; ok ? "1" : "0"; })

hints: Write two nested loops over the source: row `i`, column `j`.
`src[i][j]` lives at `src[i * cols + j]`. In the destination, which is `cols x rows`, element `[j][i]` lives at `dst[j * rows + i]`.
The destination's row length is `rows`, not `cols`. Mixing those two up passes square tests and fails rectangular ones.
explain: For every `(i, j)` the solution copies `src[i * cols + j]` into `dst[j * rows + i]`, using each array's own row length. Square matrices hide the classic bug of reusing `cols` for the destination, which is why the tests include single rows, single columns, and 2x3 shapes.
